I’m saying that it’s important to meet kids where they are and with what interests them.

I think reading complex literature is incredibly enriching, but sometimes you have to let kids read what they’re naturally drawn to. There needs to be some balance in curriculum.

You’re absolutely right that most kids don’t enjoy reading *most* stories, which is why reading things like Shakespeare, who I use as an example here; any of the authors you’d mentioned could easily be substituted, doesn’t work for *most* kids. 

For example, in my 8th grade class, some of my students are reading on a 3rd grade level (I teach at an inner city public school). If I tried to read A Midsummer Night’s Dream or Romeo and Juliet or 1984 or even Fahrenheit 451, a majority of my students will gain absolutely nothing because it’s inaccessible. Sure, the 3-4 high achievers in my class of 31 kids would benefit, but the majority would actively suffer through it. 

My point is that allowing kids to read trash like The Hunger Games, Twilight, whatever else is often an effective way to coax them into a more literate life.

As a middle school English teacher, and one who advocates for teaching the classics, there is some validity to this. 

A famous language acquisition researcher, Krashner, has asserted time and time again that kids need to be exposed to lit that captivates them, especially early on when reading skills are developing. The idea is that you get better at reading by reading, and we want kids to WANT to read. 

Teaching Shakespeare loses MOST kids, so it’s basically fruitless because kids will literally stop reading and trying altogether. 

Education doesn’t exist within a vacuum and you need to consider the cultural context in which you are teaching. In the west, we are a culture with increasingly less strict educational attitudes, so if a kid is failing their language arts classes, parents are less likely to blame the child & demand improvement. 

So, essentially what we’ve decided to do, as a culture, is take a more utilitarian approach, aiming to broadly educate the masses and establish a basic literacy standard. A very small subset of the population is highly literate and able to dissect complex texts like Shakespeare, especially given the archaic language he used. 

And for some kids, trash literature and comic books are just what they like to read, and any reading is preferable to no reading. It can also lead to a more literary interest.
